headline: High: shared filesystem and MCP create prompt-injection, leakage, and write-conflict risks; TREK’s sensitive travel data raises compliance exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can use MCP and shared filesystem state, and TREK also exposes MCP plus collaborative real-time inputs. That creates a plausible path for TREK content or files to be treated as instructions by Continue, even though no direct parser behavior is documented. The interaction is inferred from both profiles, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF Continue reads TREK-generated files or MCP payloads as instructions without provenance checks
IF both agents are connected through the same workspace or MCP server
mitigations: Disable shared MCP endpoints between the agents
Separate workspaces and mount points for each agent
Require provenance tags on all MCP/file inputs
Review any TREK-generated text before Continue consumes it

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and has broad network egress; TREK stores reservations, documents, photos, API keys, and MFA secrets in files and logs. If they share a filesystem, Continue can ingest sensitive TREK data and transmit context externally. The blast radius includes secrets and personal travel records, so this is high rather than medium.
conditions: IF Continue is pointed at the same host workspace as TREK
IF TREK files or logs contain reservations, API keys, or MFA secrets
mitigations: Use separate OS users for each agent
Place TREK data in a directory Continue cannot read
Redact secrets from TREK logs and uploads
Disable network egress for Continue when handling TREK data
Rotate any exposed API keys or MFA secrets

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, while TREK is collaborative and uses files plus WebSocket/OIDC/MCP surfaces. Both can mutate shared state via filesystem, and Continue’s session scope is per-IDE window with shared state via filesystem. Without explicit locking, concurrent writes can corrupt shared project or app data, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or database-backed workspace
IF TREK collaborative sessions and Continue sessions overlap in time
mitigations: Assign disjoint writable directories
Enable file locking around shared artifacts
Serialize edits through one agent at a time
Back up TREK data before concurrent use
Avoid letting Continue modify TREK database files

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or text from workspace context, and TREK is a real-time collaborative planner with AI built in. If TREK consumes Continue’s output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into plans, reservations, or user-facing actions. The pathway exists, but direct action authority is not fully documented, so medium fits.
conditions: IF TREK ingests Continue-produced text into planning or booking workflows
IF TREK does not verify Continue output before displaying or acting on it
mitigations: Require human review before bookings or edits
Add validation checks for dates, prices, and identifiers
Mark Continue output as untrusted in TREK
Log source provenance for imported suggestions

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly touches reservations, documents, photos, email addresses, confirmation numbers, API keys, and MFA secrets, while Continue handles workspace files and model-provider API keys. If TREK data is processed by Continue, residency and retention obligations can be breached, especially because Continue’s network egress is broad and TREK is self-hosted with sensitive travel records. The profiles do not show a shared DPA or residency control.
conditions: IF TREK personal data or secrets are routed into Continue prompts or logs
IF the deployment requires residency or retention controls not enforced by either agent
mitigations: Keep regulated travel data out of Continue prompts
Configure retention limits on TREK logs and uploads
Document data-flow boundaries between the agents
Use separate storage regions if residency matters
Review whether a DPA is required before deployment
